c1: baymutt: a secret store for coding agents
c2: A zero-knowledge secret store for people who run coding agents. See why your agent wants a secret before you approve, and hand over a new one in one paste.
c5: A mutt sitting by a bay with a key in its mouth
c6: baymutt is a secret store for coding agents. Your agent says what it needs and why. You approve, or paste a value only you can fetch.
c11: Each request shows who is asking, why in the agent’s own words, what it would reach and until when. You approve or reject on one screen, knowing what you’re saying yes to.
c13: Some values only you can fetch, like a new API key. The usual way: copy it, open your secret store, find the right environment, add a secret, name it, paste. With baymutt, your agent fills in everything it can and sends you a link. You open it and paste.
c15: Your agent asks, you approve, and that’s your part done. Within the access you approved, it reads the secrets already stored or writes new ones itself, without coming back to you each time. The activity shows each read and write.
c16: Sealed on your side. Unreadable on ours.
c18: Every value, and every environment and secret name, is sealed in your browser or on your computer before it is sent. baymutt never holds the keys, so it can’t read any of it.
c19: How the sealing works, and what it doesn’t hide
c21: The server, the dashboard and the CLI are public on GitHub under AGPL-3.0 and MIT, and this site deploys from that code. Read how the promise is kept instead of taking our word for it.
c26: Then install baymutt and log in where your agents run.
c28: baymutt sounds like 秘密 (bei mat), the Cantonese word for secret.
